title: Necrotising soft tissue infection (necrotising fasciitis)
subject: surgery-trauma
summary: A clinical diagnosis driven by pain out of proportion and rapid progression: resuscitate, start broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin or linezolid for toxin suppression, and take the patient for urgent radical debridement without waiting for imaging or scores, with planned re-look within 12 to 24 hours.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Pain out of proportion to the skin findings, rapid spread, tense oedema beyond the erythema, and systemic toxicity; early skin changes may look like simple cellulitis.
Late signs: haemorrhagic bullae, skin necrosis or grey discolouration, crepitus, skin anaesthesia, and thin grey (dishwater) discharge.

Risk factors: diabetes, obesity, immunosuppression, alcohol misuse, injecting drug use, peripheral vascular disease, and recent surgery or trauma. Fournier gangrene affects the perineum and genitalia, often in people with diabetes.

Type 1 is polymicrobial (commonest; trunk, perineum, diabetics). Type 2 is monomicrobial, usually group A streptococcus with or without S. aureus, often on limbs in healthy people. Also clostridial gas gangrene, and Vibrio (sea water) or Aeromonas (fresh water) after water exposure.
LRINEC score (CRP, WBC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose): 8 or more indicates about 75% risk, but sensitivity is poor. A low score must never exclude NSTI or delay surgery.

sections.title: First hour
items: Treat as septic shock: blood cultures, lactate, IV fluids and vasopressors as needed (see the sepsis protocol).
Call the senior surgeon immediately. Surgery must not be delayed by medical or ICU management, imaging, or inter-hospital transfer (BOAST 2025).
Start empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics immediately after blood cultures.
Mark the margins of erythema and time them, but do not wait for visible spread before acting.

sections.title: Investigations
items: The diagnosis is clinical and confirmed at surgery (fascial necrosis, loss of tissue planes, easy finger dissection).

Imaging only if the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain and it will not delay surgery: a plain X-ray cannot exclude NSTI; CT may show fascial gas or fluid; point-of-care ultrasound can help in unstable patients.
When unsure, an incisional biopsy with frozen section and Gram stain can confirm the diagnosis early.
Blood: FBC, CRP, electrolytes, creatinine, CK, glucose, coagulation, lactate, blood cultures; HbA1c in suspected diabetes.

sections.title: Source control
items: Debride as soon as possible and within 12 hours of admission at most when NSTI is strongly suspected; earlier in septic shock. Excise all necrotic tissue back to healthy, bleeding tissue and leave the wound open.
Take multiple deep tissue samples (ideally 5, from different zones) for Gram stain and culture, labelled as necrotising infection.
Plan the first re-exploration within 12 to 24 hours and repeat until no necrosis remains; failure to improve implies incomplete debridement.
Amputation decisions should involve at least two consultants. In Fournier gangrene with faecal soiling, consider faecal diversion (colostomy or a faecal management system).
Negative pressure wound therapy may be used once all necrotic tissue is removed.

sections.title: Antibiotics
items: Empirical (IDSA 2014): vancomycin or linezolid plus piperacillin-tazobactam, or plus a carbapenem, or plus ceftriaxone and metronidazole. Include clindamycin or linezolid for toxin suppression (WSES/SIS-E 2018).
In Indian hospitals with high ESBL prevalence, a carbapenem (meropenem) is often the gram-negative backbone; follow the local antibiogram.
Confirmed group A streptococcus or clostridial infection: benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin.
Vibrio vulnificus: doxycycline plus ceftriaxone or cefotaxime. Aeromonas: doxycycline plus ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone.
Continue until no further debridement is needed, the patient has improved clinically, and fever has settled for 48 to 72 hours; de-escalate by cultures.

sections.title: Adjuncts and supportive care
items: IV immunoglobulin: consider only for group A streptococcal NSTI, especially with toxic shock (weak recommendation, limited evidence); it never replaces surgery.
Hyperbaric oxygen: optional after debridement if already available on site; never delay surgery or transfer for it.
ICU care, early enteral nutrition, and glucose control; review by the treating team within 6 hours of diagnosis or surgery.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Labelling it cellulitis because the skin looks unimpressive.
Waiting for CT, the LRINEC score or skin necrosis before operating.
An inadequate first debridement or no planned re-look.
Missing Fournier gangrene in a diabetic patient with perineal pain.
Omitting clindamycin or linezolid in streptococcal or clostridial infection.

drugs.name: Vancomycin
drugs.dose: 30 mg/kg/day IV in 2 divided doses (15 mg/kg every 12 hours), adjusted to levels
drugs.notes: MRSA cover; adjust for renal function.

drugs.name: Linezolid
drugs.notes: MRSA cover with toxin suppression; can replace vancomycin plus clindamycin.

drugs.name: Piperacillin-tazobactam
drugs.dose: 3.375 g IV every 6 to 8 hours (IDSA 2014); 4.5 g IV every 6 to 8 hours is widely used in severe sepsis
drugs.notes: Gram-negative and anaerobic cover; reduce dose in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Meropenem
drugs.notes: Preferred where ESBL risk is high; reduce dose in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Clindamycin
drugs.notes: Toxin suppression in streptococcal and clostridial infection.

drugs.name: Benzylpenicillin
drugs.dose: 2 to 4 million units (1.2 to 2.4 g) IV every 4 to 6 hours
drugs.notes: With clindamycin for group A streptococcal or clostridial infection.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole
drugs.dose: Ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g IV every 24 hours plus metronidazole 500 mg IV every 6 to 8 hours
drugs.notes: Alternative gram-negative and anaerobic backbone with an anti-MRSA agent.
